title: Getting started
summary: What Woodshop is and the ways to start your first design.

blocks.text: Woodshop turns a furniture idea into a real, buildable design: a 3D model you can spin around, plus an automatic cut list of every board to buy and cut. Everything runs on this computer — there is no account, no subscription, and nothing leaves your machine unless you export it.
Ways to start

items: Take the tour. Help ▸ Take the tour opens a sample nightstand and walks through the editor in five short steps.
Start from a template. The Templates gallery has 30 ready-made designs (side table, bookshelf, dresser, workbench, and more). Pick one and it opens in the editor as your own copy.
Start blank. Create a project and build it up part by part from the Add menu.
Import a file. Open a .woodshop project someone sent you (or double-click it), or a spec JSON exported from the web version of Woodshop.
Let your own AI agent build it. Connect Claude Desktop or Claude Code over MCP (see Connect your own AI agent) and describe what you want.

blocks.text: How a design is stored

Every design is a set of parts, materials, and joints — measured in inches. Woodshop draws the 3D model and the cut list from that description, so the two are always in sync. You never edit raw 3D shapes; you change the design and everything updates.

Your projects live in a single library on this computer, backed up automatically (see Saving, versions & backups). To move a project to another machine or send it to someone, use Save project file in the ⋯ menu on its card.
Inches or millimetres

Settings ▸ General ▸ Units chooses how sizes are shown and typed: inches as fractions, decimal inches, or millimetres. Any size field also takes a unit you type, such as 450 mm or 17 3/4 in. Designs are stored the same way whichever you pick, so you can switch at any time.

title: The 3D editor
summary: Move, resize, and join parts; undo and version history.

blocks.text: The editor is where you see and shape a design. The 3D view shows the assembled piece; the inspector shows the selected part and its dimensions.

blocks.alt: The editor: the parts list on the left, the 3D view in the middle, the cut list on the right.
blocks.caption: The parts list, the 3D view and the cut list. The badge at the bottom left says whether the design can be built.

blocks.text: Working with parts

items: Click a part to select it; Shift-click to add more. The Inspector shows its size, material and position.
Resize a part by typing its length and width. Thickness comes from the material.
Move a part by dragging it, by typing its position, or with the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps, Alt for smaller, Page Up and Page Down for height).
Turn it with Tip, Turn and Roll in the Inspector.
Add parts from the Add menu: legs, aprons, slats, panels, shelves, boards and dowel rails, each at a sensible starting size.
Make a row of the same part, such as slats, shelves or legs, with Copies… in the Inspector: how many, which way, and the gap between them.

Build one side and let the app make the other: select a part, a group or several parts and choose Left ↔ right, Front ↔ back or Top ↔ bottom under Mirrored copy. The copy lands on the far side of the design's middle, turned so its cuts, edge banding and hardware face the mirror-image way, and named for its side (Left Side becomes Right Side).

Cover the plywood edges that will show with edge banding: the Inspector's Edge banding section has a button for each edge, the banded edges show as a pale strip in 3D, and the cut list adds up how much to buy.
Select three or more parts and choose Space evenly to spread them out with equal gaps, keeping the two outer ones where they are. Handy for shelves between a bottom and a top.
Select several parts and press ⌘G to group them, so they select and move together.

blocks.text: The parts list

The list on the left shows every part: doors and drawers first, each with the parts it is built from, then groups, then the rest. Click a name to select that part, even one hidden inside the design; double-click to rename it; use the eye to hide it from view and bring it back. Show or hide the list with Parts in the toolbar, or P.
Views and shortcuts

The buttons over the 3D view look from the front, the side or the top, go back to the three-quarter view, or fit the whole design in view; with parts selected, Selected zooms in on them. Press ? or the ? button for every keyboard shortcut. The ones you will use most: E explodes the view, O opens the doors and drawers, M measures, F zooms to the selection (or fits the design in view when nothing is selected), V switches between Edit and View, H hides the selection, and ⌘Z undoes.
Joinery

How parts are joined (dados, pocket screws, screws and dowels) and the shaping cut into them are covered in Cuts, joinery & fasteners. A part that only rests against its neighbours is not held by anything, and the design checks will say so.
Undo and safety
Every change can be undone. Your work autosaves as you go, and you can save named versions to go back to (see Versions & autosave).
The 3D view has two modes: View (orbit and zoom the camera only) and Edit (select, drag and change parts). Switch with the Edit/View toggle in the toolbar so a drag does what you expect.

title: Doors & drawers
summary: Turn a panel into a door or a drawer, choose its hinges, slides and pull, and see it open.

blocks.text: A door is a panel on hinges; a drawer is a front with a box behind it on slides. Woodshop knows which parts belong to which, swings and slides them, places their hardware and checks that it fits.

blocks.alt: A nightstand with its drawer pulled open; the Inspector shows the drawer's style, slides and pull.
blocks.caption: Press O, or Open in the toolbar, to see doors swing and drawers slide. The slider sets how far.

blocks.text: Make one

items: Select the parts around an opening (two sides, a bottom and a top, say) and choose Add ▸ Door or Add ▸ Drawer. Woodshop sizes it from the opening.
Or choose Add ▸ Door or Drawer with nothing selected and type the opening's width and height.
Or select a panel that is already the right size and choose Make a door or Make a drawer in the Inspector.

blocks.text: Inset doors and fronts sit inside the opening with a 1/16" reveal all round; overlay ones lap the opening by 1/2" a side. A new drawer's box leaves the 1/2" each side that side-mount slides need.
Hinges, slides and pulls

Select any part of a door or drawer and use its section of the Inspector: the style, which edge the hinges are on, the hinge or slides, and the pull. Woodshop places them and moves them as the door swings or the drawer slides. Choose None for a push latch or a wooden pull.
Pick a concealed (Euro) hinge and Woodshop bores its 35 mm cups in the door for you. They show in 3D, on the shop template and in the plan's Drilling section, and move if you resize the door.
What gets checked

items: A door too thin for its hinge cups.
A drawer box that does not leave its side-mount slides their clearance, with the width to make it.
A drawer on undermount slides without the 1/2" recess under its bottom.
A lid, or a door hinged along its top, with nothing to hold it open: add a lid stay.

blocks.text: Dissolve, in the door or drawer section, turns it back into ordinary parts.

title: Cuts, joinery & fasteners
summary: Dados, rabbets, holes, pocket screws, curves, notches, miters and soft edges, and how parts are held together.

blocks.text: A part starts as a plain rectangle. Cuts shape it and join it to its neighbours: they show in 3D, on the shop templates and in the PDF, and the hardware list counts the screws and dowels.

blocks.alt: The Cuts & fasteners section for a shelf: pocket screws and two rows of screws, + Add a cut, and Fasten to buttons for each neighbouring part.

blocks.text: Add a cut
Select a part and choose + Add a cut in the Inspector:

items: **Dado or groove**: a channel another part sits in.
**Rabbet**: a step along an edge, for a back panel or a lid to sit in. Set the panel into it and the joint is recorded.
**Hole**: for a dowel, a shelf pin, or right through.

**Rows of holes**: two columns of holes up a case side for adjustable shelves. They start on the 32 mm system, on the face that looks into the case, and the whole run shows as one line you can change or delete. Choose hinge plates & slides to drill the same rows for the screws of cup-hinge mounting plates and drawer slides, often only the column by the front edge.
**Pocket screws**: angled screws through an edge into the next part.
**Curve**: an arched edge or rounded corners.
**Notch**: a cut-out from an edge, for example round a leg.
**Miter**: an angled edge for a corner joint.
**Soft edge**: a roundover, chamfer or bullnose.

blocks.text: Each cut is listed in plain words, such as "2 screws, #8 × 1 1/2", through the back face". Click one to change it: its form opens with its sizes filled in, and Save changes puts the new ones in its place. The × beside one removes it. Screws through a face, which Fasten to adds, are removed and added again rather than changed.
Fasten to

Touching is not holding. Under Fasten to, the Inspector lists every part this one meets; choose Pocket screws, Screws or Dowels and Woodshop picks the size for the thicknesses involved, places them, and adds them to the hardware list. A part that is not fastened to anything is flagged by the design checks.
Joints are notes on the design about how pieces connect. Moving a part never secretly moves its neighbours, but the checks will tell you if a screw no longer reaches anything.

title: Adding hardware
summary: Pulls, hinges, slides, casters and more: real sizes, shown in 3D and counted in the hardware list.

blocks.text: Woodshop has a catalog of real hardware with true dimensions: knobs and pulls, hinges, drawer slides, casters, leveling feet, brackets and plates, shelf pins, latches, lid stays and handles, and hooks. Hardware shows in the 3D view, moves with the part it is screwed to, and is counted in the hardware list, so the cut list, PDF and CSV tell you what to buy. Pulls, knobs and hinges can be finished in satin nickel, matte black, brass or oil-rubbed bronze: pick a Finish on a door or drawer, or on any piece in a part's hardware list. The 3D view shows the colour and the hardware list names it.

blocks.alt: The Add hardware dialog, with a 128 mm bar pull picked and a preview of it.

blocks.text: Put hardware on a part

items: Open Add ▸ Hardware… in the editor toolbar, or select a part and choose + Add hardware in the inspector.
Pick a category or search, and click an item to see a preview and its size.

Choose Place on the model, then click where it goes on a part: a face, an edge or an end. Press R to turn it a quarter turn. You can keep clicking to place more; press Esc or Done when you are finished.
Or pick a part under "Or add to the centre of" and choose Add to drop it in the middle of that part's front face.

blocks.text: Move, turn or remove it

Drag a piece in the 3D view to slide it along the face it is on. It snaps to the face's centre lines, to the row or column other hardware on that face sits on, and to the same piece on a matching door or drawer front, so pulls line up across a run of drawers. The label shows how far it is from the two near edges. Hold Alt (Option on a Mac) to drag freely, press Esc to put it back, and Undo takes back the whole drag.

Click a piece in the 3D view, or select its part, to see it in the inspector's Hardware section. There you can change which side it is on (front or back face, an edge, or an end), type its position in inches, turn it 90°, or remove it. Casters and feet usually go on an end: the end of a leg or the bottom edge of a base. On an edge or an end, a piece placed near the middle of the thickness snaps to its centre line.
Doors and drawers

A door's hinges and pull, and a drawer's slides and pull, are chosen on the door or drawer itself, and Woodshop places them for you (see Doors & drawers). Choose None for a push latch or a wooden pull.

Choose a concealed (Euro) hinge for a door and Woodshop bores its 35 mm cups for you: they show in the door, on its shop template and in the plan's Drilling section, and move if you resize the door or change the hinge. Other hardware never cuts the part, so a pull's screw holes are holes you add from the inspector's cuts. Casters and feet do add to the overall height shown in the cut list.

title: Design checks
summary: What "Buildable" means, the problems Woodshop looks for, and the sturdiness advice.

blocks.text: Woodshop checks the design every time it changes. The badge at the bottom left of the 3D view says Buildable when nothing stops you building it, or how many errors there are. Click it to see each finding; click a finding to select the part it is about.

blocks.alt: The editor with the design checks open: two advisories say the screws on the open shelf no longer reach another part.
blocks.caption: Here the shelf was lifted off its cleats, so its screws fasten nothing.

blocks.text: Errors

Errors are things that cannot be built as drawn: a part bigger than the sheet or board it is cut from, a part fastened to nothing, two parts in the same space, a cut that runs off the part. The PDF plan and the cut list still work, but fix these before you cut wood.
Warnings

Warnings are things that can be built but probably should not be: screws that reach nothing, a door too thin for its hinges, a drawer box the wrong width for its slides, a lid with no stay. Each says what to change.
Sturdiness advice

Advisories estimate how the piece will hold up: a shelf that may sag under load (and what span would not), a tall piece that could tip and should be anchored to the wall, an open frame that may rack without a back or stretchers, a long thin part that may flex. They use the same maths as the shop calculators.
A connected AI agent runs the same checks with `check_design`, so it fixes what you would.

title: Cut lists & exports
summary: Every board to cut, board feet, sheet layouts, and a printable plan.

blocks.text: The cut list is generated from your design — it is always up to date. It lists every part, how many to cut, its dimensions, and the material.

blocks.alt: The cut list panel: overall size, board feet, sheets, cost, offcut and the parts on each material.

blocks.text: What it shows

items: Totals: the overall size and about what the wood weighs, board feet, sheets, an estimated cost once you add prices, and how much of the stock ends up as offcut. The weight uses a typical density for each material (from its name or species) and leaves out the hardware, so treat it as an estimate. Under it, the surface to finish (both faces and every edge) and about how much finish a coat takes, at 100 square feet a quart: right for a brushed polyurethane or paint, generous for an oil.
Each material with its parts underneath, largest first. Identical parts are counted once with ×2, ×4 and so on.

Sheet goods (plywood, MDF): how many sheets and how the parts are laid out on them, grain-aware. Tick **Show the cut order** to number the saw cuts: rip each sheet into strips, then crosscut the strips; under each layout every cut is listed with its fence setting, the width of the piece it takes off. Boards are numbered too: crosscut to rough length first, then ripped, each cut with its stop or fence setting.

**Joinery** folds out the tool setups the design needs (each dado stack, bit and blade angle, with how many cuts are made at it) and then each part's dados, grooves, rabbets, holes and shaping in words, as the PDF plan prints them.
In the shop, tick each row as you cut it: the layouts fade the pieces that are done and a line counts them. Ticks are remembered for each design on this computer; **Clear** starts again.

Lumber: each board drawn with the parts cut from it. When the material gives a board width, narrow parts are ripped side by side if that buys fewer boards. When a material is sold in more than one length, each board is bought at the shortest length its cuts fit.

Fasteners and hardware: every screw, dowel, hinge, slide and pull the design uses, folded under Fasteners until you need it. Edge banding is listed here too, in whole feet or metres with a little spare.

blocks.text: Cutting allows for a saw kerf (the width of material the blade removes) between pieces, so the plan reflects what you can really get out of a sheet or board. Under **Stock & kerf**, **Trim sheet edges** takes 1/8" to 1/2" off every edge of a bought sheet before the parts, for factory edges that are dinged or out of square: the layouts draw the trimmed edges dashed and measure each cut from them. **Trim board ends** does the same for boards, 1/2" to 2" off each end, for ends that are checked or sniped. A material with a part as big as the whole sheet or as long as its longest board is left whole, and dowels are never trimmed.
Prices

Under each material, set the thickness the stock really measures (3/4" plywood is often 23/32"): the dados and rabbets its parts sit in are resized to match. Type a price next to each material: per sheet, and for boards and dowels per board foot or per board, whichever the store gives (a 2x4 at $4.48 a board is worked out per board foot from its shortest length on sale). Above the price, type the lengths a board or dowel is sold in, separated by commas, and a board's width. Choose **Add prices** above the hardware to price pulls, hinges, slides, screws and edge banding (each, or per foot or metre of banding). Hardware prices are one list for all your designs, so a price you enter once costs every design that uses the same thing. The estimated cost adds up both, and the PDF plan and CSV show what each line of hardware costs.
Stock on hand

Got part sheets and short boards left from other jobs? Add them under **On hand** in the cut list: the material, its length and, for sheet goods, its width. The cut list cuts from them before it has you buy anything, so a piece that fits there costs nothing and can save a whole sheet; each one used is drawn after the bought sheets and marked “used here”. The list is shared by every design, and the PDF plan and part labels use it too. Leftovers worth keeping (at least 12" × 6" of sheet, or 12" of board) are outlined with dashes on the layouts. Once you've cut the design, **Keep the leftovers** puts them on the list for your next job and takes off the pieces it used.
Shopping for several designs

Building more than one thing? **Shopping list** on the projects page makes one list for the designs you tick. The same material in two designs is bought once, with all their pieces packed onto shared sheets and boards, so one design's offcut can be another's shelf; it says how many sheets or boards that saves. Hardware is added up and priced from the same price list, and the last line is the finish for them all: the area and about how much a coat takes. **Save as CSV** writes it out for a spreadsheet or the store.
Printable plan

The PDF button saves a plan to take to the shop or the lumberyard: the parts table, the sheet layouts with their saw cuts numbered, the board layouts, each part's joinery and shaping in words (dados, grooves, rabbets, holes, miters, notches, curves and eased edges, worded as the Inspector words them, after a table of tool setups so each dado stack, bit and blade angle is set once), the drilling, the hardware to buy, and an order to put it together in: up from the floor, the back last, then drawers, doors and hardware, with how each part is fastened. The same order is under Assembly order at the foot of the cut list. The 3D button saves an interactive plan you can open in any browser, and CSV a spreadsheet of the cut list.
Other exports
The ⋯ menu in the editor's toolbar has every export:

items: Interactive 3D plan (HTML): a view-only copy of the design that opens in any browser, with the cut list and each part's details. Send it to a tablet for the shop: tap a part to see its sizes and joinery, tick pieces off as you cut them, and choose Keep screen on so it does not lock between cuts.
Cut list (CSV): one row per blank, in your units, for a spreadsheet.

Part labels (PDF): one sticky label per piece, with its name, size, material and the sheet or board it comes from, in the order the pieces are cut, so you can stick each on as it comes off the saw. Prints on 30-up US Letter label sheets (Avery 5160 and the like), or 21-up A4 sheets (Avery L7160) if you work in millimetres. On a sheet you've started, click the first free label and printing starts there.
Shop templates (SVG): full-size printable patterns for shaped and drilled parts.

Parts for CNC (DXF): every part laid flat, front face up, for CAM software such as VCarve, Fusion or Easel. The outline is on layer CUT_OUTSIDE; holes and dados are on layers named by depth (HOLE_0.5, POCKET_0.375, HOLE_THROUGH), and _BACK marks one cut from the back face, which means flipping the part. Concealed-hinge cups are included. Sizes are in millimetres if you work in metric, inches otherwise.
3D model (glTF): the assembled design, hardware included, for Blender, SketchUp, Fusion or a 3D viewer.

blocks.text: A connected AI agent can fetch the parts table and board feet with the `get_cut_list` tool; the full packed sheet layout lives here in the app.

title: Saving, versions & backups
summary: Autosave, named versions, automatic backups of the whole library, and project files.

blocks.text: You do not need to hit save. The editor autosaves your working design a moment after you stop making changes, and reopening a project restores exactly where you left off.
Version history

blocks.alt: The version history panel with one saved version, "Before the drawer", and its Restore button.

items: Save a version to bookmark a design you like before experimenting.
Before a connected AI agent changes a design, Woodshop snapshots your current design automatically — labelled so you can find it.
Restore any earlier version to roll back; restoring makes it your current working design.

blocks.text: If an AI agent edits the project you have open, the editor picks the change up. If you had unsaved edits at the same moment, Woodshop asks whether to keep yours or take the other, so nothing is silently lost.
Backups of the whole library

Woodshop copies your whole library once a day, the first time a few seconds after it starts, and keeps the last week of copies. Settings ▸ Library ▸ Backups lists them; Back up now makes one straight away. Open a backup to see the projects in it and restore any one of them: it comes back as a new project named "(restored)", so nothing you have now is replaced.
Project files

Save project file, in the ⋯ menu on a project card or in the editor, writes a single .woodshop file with the design, its versions and its notes. Send it to someone, keep it somewhere safe, or move it to another computer; Import… on the Projects page (or double-clicking the file) brings it back.

title: Using Woodshop with an AI agent
summary: Chat with the built-in design assistant, or let Claude Desktop, Claude Code or another MCP client build in Woodshop.

blocks.text: Woodshop works with AI in two ways: a design assistant built into the editor, and an MCP server that runs on this computer, so your own AI agent (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, an IDE assistant, or something you build) can list, read, create, and edit your designs. The MCP server needs no account or token — it only ever talks to the library on this machine.
The design assistant, inside the editor

The quickest way in: the editor's **Assistant** tab is a chat about the design you have open. Ask for a change in plain words and the assistant makes it with the same tools an MCP agent uses, so every change is checked, lands in the editor straight away, and is saved as a version you can go back to.

items: Get an API key from console.anthropic.com (or use an OpenAI-compatible server, such as OpenAI or a local Ollama).
In Settings ▸ AI agents ▸ Design assistant, choose the provider and model and paste the key. It is kept in your system keychain, not in Woodshop's library.

Open a design, click the Assistant tab and ask. Enter sends; Shift+Enter starts a new line. Stop ends a long answer after the step it is on. Turn on Show the view to send a picture of the 3D view with your message, for questions about how it looks. A reply that changed the design has **Undo these changes**, which puts the design back as it was before that reply (Versions keeps both). Each design keeps its own chat, so you can come back to it later; New chat starts over.

blocks.text: While you use the assistant, your messages and the parts of the design it reads are sent to the provider you chose, and its use is billed to your key. Nothing is sent until you send a message.
Your own agent, over MCP

blocks.alt: Settings ▸ AI agents, with the configuration for Claude Desktop and the command for Claude Code, each with a Copy button.

blocks.text: Set it up

items: Open Settings → AI agents (MCP) and copy the configuration shown there.
Paste it into your MCP client's configuration (for Claude Desktop: Settings → Developer → Edit Config). It launches Woodshop with `--mcp` as a local stdio server.
Restart the client. Ask it to `list_projects` to check the connection.

blocks.text: What the agent can do

items: Read: `list_projects`, `get_design`, `get_cut_list`, `check_design`, `explain_part`.
Start: `start_design` (a blank design) or `start_from_template`.
Exact edits: `add_part`, `resize_part`, `move_part`, `add_op`, `add_joint`, `set_material`, `delete_part`, and more — every edit is validated against the same rules as the editor.

blocks.text: What to ask

Describe the piece the way you would to a friend who builds furniture, with the sizes you care about. The agent reads Woodshop's conventions first, builds the design part by part, and runs the same design checks you see in the editor.

items: "Start a 30 inch wide bookshelf, 12 deep, with four adjustable shelves in oak plywood."
"Make the drawer in my nightstand an inch deeper and fix whatever that breaks."
"Why does my workbench say it might rack? Add what it needs."
"What should I buy for the media console? Give me the cut list and the hardware."

blocks.text: Open the project in Woodshop while the agent works and you see each change as it lands.
Parts the agent leaves alone

A part you adjust by hand (resize it, change its material, add a cut to it) is **locked**: the assistant and any agent leave it exactly as it is, and a change that would move, resize, re-cut, rename or delete it is refused. Joints to it and hardware on it can still be added. The lock shows beside the part's name in the Inspector and in the parts list; click it to unlock the part and let the agent change it, or to lock any part you want kept as it is.
Every agent edit is saved as a version first, so you can always restore what you had. The agent works on your library even while the app is closed.

title: Shop calculators
summary: Fourteen calculators for the numbers you work out at the bench — no project needed.

blocks.text: Everything else in Woodshop works from a design. The calculators do not: they take numbers you type and hand back an answer, so you can reach for them with nothing open. Find them under **Tools**, or from the ⋯ menu in the editor toolbar while you are working.
Typing measurements

Every dimension field reads fractions the way you write them: `3/4`, `1 1/2`, `1-1/2`, or plain decimals like `12.5`. Nothing complains while you are mid-word — `1 1/` is part of typing `1 1/2` — and when you leave the field it tidies what you typed, so `0.375` becomes `3/8`. Where a field offers units, switching converts the value rather than the digits.
What is here

items: **Material & stock** — board feet and cost for a pile of rough lumber; how many boards or sheets your parts cut from, kerf included; and a converter that also shows how far your fraction rounds off.
**Strength & seasonal movement** — whether a shelf will sag under load and the longest span that still passes; and how much a solid panel grows and shrinks between winter and summer.
**Joinery** — mortise and tenon proportions, dowel size and spacing, and pilot, clearance and countersink sizes for a screw in your species.
**Angles, curves & proportion** — saw settings for any number of sides (flat or canted), arcs from a chord and rise, segmented rings, leg tapers and splays, and proportion helpers.

blocks.text: They agree with the rest of the app

The shelf-sag calculator uses the same maths as the sturdiness warnings in the editor, and the pilot-hole calculator sizes screws with the same rules that draw them on your design. So a calculator will never tell you something different from what the editor tells you about the same shelf or the same joint.
They never touch your project

The calculators do not read your design and cannot change it. Opening them from the editor puts them over the canvas without navigating away — your selection, camera and undo history are exactly where you left them when you close it.
A stock estimate counts the saw kerf between every cut, which is why two 48-inch pieces do not come out of one 96-inch board.
